name: Password storage and authentication-scheme analysis
identify_givens: A password database with U users whose passwords come from a known list of L candidates, a concrete storage formula built from a secure hash H and concatenation (e.g. H(password), H(username++password), H(H(username)++password), H(username++H(password))), and an attacker Mallory who can read and modify the database; or a Lamport-style hash-chain registration/login scheme using H^k(pwd||salt) with a server-side 'stored' variable and a network or server-compromising attacker. Only hash computations count as cost; comparisons and database operations are free.
identify_target: For each storage scheme, describe the attack and compute the exact number of hash evaluations needed (a) to recover every user's password and (b) to change every password to a new value like 'pwned'; or, for hash-chain schemes, justify what the server must know, compute the chain index/cost of the next login, state at which login an eavesdropper learns the password, and show how a server-compromising attacker logs in without pwd/salt/i.

algorithm.detail: Write down the exact stored-value formula, the attacker's capabilities (read DB, modify DB, eavesdrop, compromise server), and the goal (recover all passwords, or set all passwords to a fixed new value such as pwned).

Split the hash expression into user-independent subexpressions that can be precomputed once and reused (e.g. $H(password)$ is the same for all users; a dictionary of all $L$ values of $H(password)$ costs $L$ hashes once) and per-user subexpressions that must be recomputed for each user (anything concatenated with the username or per-user salt).

For each of the $U$ users, test all $L$ candidate passwords against the stored value; total = (one-time precomputation) + $U \times L \times$ (hashes per candidate after reuse). E.g. unsalted: $L$; salted outer hash: $U \cdot L$; inner hashed username: $U + U \cdot L$; inner hashed password: $L + U \cdot L$.

Apply the same factoring to the new password pwned: compute its user-independent inner hash once if the formula needs it, then one outer hash per user. E.g. unsalted: $1$; salted: $U$; $H(H(user)++pwd)$: $U + U = 2U$; $H(user++H(pwd))$: $1 + U$. Note pwned is not in the list, so its hash cannot come from the dictionary precomputation.

If a goal requires inverting H (recovering pwd from a hash outside the candidate list, or reversing a hash chain), state it is infeasible because H is one-way; state that the server only needs to know the values it actually compares, not pwd or salt.

For Lamport-style schemes where login $i$ sends $H^{N-i}(pwd\|salt)$ and the server checks $H(\text{received}) = stored$ then updates $stored$: the next login needs exponent $N-i-1$, which cannot be derived from the sent value (one-wayness) and costs full recomputation from pwd; at login $N$ the client sends $H^0(pwd\|salt) = pwd\|salt$ in plaintext; an attacker who can write $stored$ sets $stored = H(v)$ for a chosen $v$ and logs in with $v$.

Give the final count per scheme and per goal as a closed formula in $U$ and $L$ (e.g. $L$, $1$, $U \cdot L$, $U$, $U + U \cdot L$, $2U$, $L + U \cdot L$, $U + 1$), with one line of justification each; remember only hash evaluations count, comparisons and DB writes are free.

variations.name: Hash placement / nesting
variations.detail: The professor permutes where H and the username sit: H(password), H(username++password), H(H(username)++password), H(username++H(password)). Where the inner hash sits decides what is reusable: a dictionary of H(pwd) is reusable across users only when H(pwd) appears as an inner term (giving L + U*L instead of U*L); H(username) is precomputable once per user (adding U). Trap: forgetting that pwned is not in the L-list, so its inner hash costs one extra evaluation in the replacement attack (U+1, not U).

variations.name: Lamport hash-chain login
variations.detail: Instead of a static database, the scheme sends H^(N-i)(pwd||salt) at login i and the server verifies H(received)=stored. Sub-questions ask whether the server needs pwd/salt (no — it only compares hashes), the cost of the next login (full recomputation, chain cannot be walked backwards), when an eavesdropper learns pwd (at i=N, since H^0(x)=x is sent in plaintext), and the server-compromise attack (set stored=H(v), log in with v). Trap: thinking the next token can be derived from the current one — one-wayness forbids it.

variations.name: Role reversal: attacker writes the database
variations.detail: The second goal always flips the attacker from reader to writer: instead of cracking, Mallory replaces stored hashes so every user has password pwned. The cost structure mirrors recovery but with L replaced by the single value pwned. Trap: reusing the dictionary of L password hashes for pwned, or forgetting the per-user salt forces U separate outer hashes.

variations.name: Design-critique checklist
variations.detail: Other sittings list organizational measures (secret proprietary hash, one global 'salt', strict composition rules, forced rotation, lockout, phone recovery) and ask which attack each counters. Map each: proprietary hash violates Kerckhoffs' principle; a global salt is not a salt and does not stop rainbow tables — only per-user salts do; lockout stops online guessing but enables user-targeted DoS; slow KDF raises offline cracking cost. Adapt by naming the attack each measure does and does not address.

example_problem: Alice maintains a password database with U users; each user has a unique username and picks a password from a list of L passwords; H is a secure cryptographic hash. Mallory can read and modify the database and wants to (1) compute every user's password and (2) change every user's password to pwned (not in the list). For each storage scheme, describe the attacks and give the number of hashes needed: 2a) store username and H(password); 2b) username and H(username++password); 2c) username and H(H(username)++password); 2d) username and H(username++H(password)).

example_steps.work: Goal (1): recover all U passwords; goal (2): overwrite all stored hashes so every password becomes pwned. Only hash computations count; comparisons and DB modifications are free.

Factoring: in 2a and 2d the inner term H(password) is user-independent, so one dictionary of all L values of H(password) is reusable across users. In 2b-2d the outer hash mixes in the username, forcing per-user recomputation. In 2c the inner H(username) is constant per user and precomputable once per user.

Recovery costs — 2a: hash each of the L candidate passwords once and compare with all stored hashes: L hashes. 2b: the salt (username) kills reuse, so hash the whole list per user: U x L hashes. 2c: precompute the U hashed usernames, then per user hash H(username)++candidate for all L candidates: U + U x L hashes. 2d: precompute the L hashed passwords, then per user hash username++H(candidate): L + U x L hashes.

Replacement costs — 2a: compute H(pwned) once and write it everywhere: 1 hash. 2b: hash username++pwned per user: U hashes. 2c: precompute U hashed usernames, then hash each with pwned: U + U = 2U hashes. 2d: compute H(pwned) once, then hash username++H(pwned) per user: U + 1 hashes.
Totals: 2a: L and 1; 2b: U x L and U; 2c: U + U x L and 2U; 2d: L + U x L and U + 1. Each attack then compares with (or overwrites) the database entries, which costs nothing under the stated model.
